query: For as-deposited, non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys in the form of nanoscale thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their magnetocaloric response and hysteresis during low-applied-field magnetic-cooling cycles, given that the notable response reported for bulk forms may not persist in a genuinely low-dimensional state and that heat-transfer rate limits cycle frequency? Specify one controlled intervention, predicted observations relative to the as-deposited baseline, applicable operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that interface‐induced magnetic frustration and constrained lattice transformations at sub‐200 nm thickness in as‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi high‐entropy alloy films reduce the magnetocaloric response and increase hysteresis under low fields relative to bulk forms. This suppression is expected to be most pronounced in films below 50 nm, where the peak magnetocaloric effect likely decreases by approximately 10–20% compared to the 200 nm baseline and hysteresis worsens at elevated cycling frequencies due to limited heat transfer.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐deposited, non‐equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi‐type HEA nanoscale thin films or lithographically patterned nanoribbons with thicknesses from 20 nm to 200 nm.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary film thickness from 20 nm to 200 nm using the same deposition conditions; perform magnetometry and direct magnetocaloric measurements from 100 K to 350 K at up to 1 T and cycle frequencies of 1–10 Hz.
generation.conditions: Compare magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of the as‐deposited 200 nm reference with thinner samples, using identical substrates and sputtering settings, to isolate thickness effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Film thickness modifies surface‐to‐volume ratio and imposes strain near interfaces, which can limit magneto‐structural transitions in thinner layers.
generation.mechanism: Magnetic and structural inhomogeneities at interfaces impede cooperative spin alignment, diminishing the magnetocaloric effect. Thinner films also exhibit lower thermal conductivity and higher demagnetizing fields, intensifying hysteresis and limiting feasible cycling rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Thinner films (<50 nm) display a measurable reduction (on the order of 10–20%) in magnetocaloric magnitude relative to the 200 nm baseline, along with increased hysteresis, particularly at cycle frequencies ≥1 Hz.
generation.baseline: Magnetocaloric performance and hysteresis in a 200 nm as‐deposited FeMnNiGeSi film measured at 100–350 K under ≤1 T fields and operating frequencies near 1–10 Hz.
generation.boundary: Effects may vary outside 20–200 nm or if the alloy composition, substrate, or deposition routes differ. Low‐field (<1 T) cooling cycles, up to ∼10 Hz, are considered due to practical application constraints.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitudes for film suppressions are not experimentally confirmed in this composition; the 10–20% estimate stems from analogous phenomena reported in related thin‐film magnetocaloric systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate multiple FeMnNiGeSi thin‐film samples of varying thickness (for instance, 20 nm, 50 nm, 100 nm, and 200 nm) under identical deposition conditions. Measure magnetocaloric properties and magnetic hysteresis loops under 0 to 1 T applied fields across 100–350 K and at 1–10 Hz cycling frequencies to appraise any thickness‐dependent changes in ΔT (or ΔS) and the loop area.
measurements: Verification of thickness (e.g., by cross‐sectional electron microscopy or X‐ray reflectivity)
Direct magnetocaloric (ΔT or ΔS) measurements under low‐field operation
Frequency‐dependent hysteresis characteristics (M–H loop measurements at multiple cycling rates)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: A lack of thickness‐dependent suppression of magnetocaloric response or an absence of worsening hysteresis at reduced film thicknesses would refute the proposed mechanism linking interface‐induced anisotropy and restricted heat transfer to diminished magnetocaloric performance.

cited_evidence.text: Relative cooling powers (RCP) for equivalent bulk and nano-sized compounds are comparable in value: 166 J/kg vs. 175 J/kg (4 T) for bulk and nano-sized with x = 0.02 This is due to the wide effective temperature range of entropy change δTFWHM in nanocrystalline samples. All values of RCP are high and comparable with relevant compounds reported in the literature. Bulk samples with x = 0.3 exhibits positive entropy change at antiferromagnetic-ferromagnetic transition temperature Magnetic entropy changes and magnetic parameters of the bulk polycrystalline samples indicate them as potential candidates for magnetocaloric materials. Possibly, they can be combined in construction of multistep refrigeration processes to increase their temperature range and effectiveness. The nanocrystalline samples, which show comparatively lower maximum entropy change are moved to the immediate background of the picture of usable magnetocaloric compounds but could, possibly, be still useful in future developments.

We have attempted to measure a magnetic moment from these films but were not able to detect a measurable signal. This suggests that the total volume fraction of spinel regions is too small for a VSM measurement. Prior work by Meisenheimer et al. and Kotsonis et al. has shown that Co3+in the rock salt structure dilutes the density of magnetic species and leads to increased magnetic frustration as it is in a low-spin configuration without an atomic moment. We note that the spinel precipitates are a few unit cells in size and therefore unlikely able to support coherent ferrimagnetism but are likely to yield uncompensated magnetic moments that can influence the exchange bias and the bulk magnetic anisotropy of the film. The exchange bias effect is dominantly interfacial with a contribution of the bulk magnetic anisotropy of the HEO that extends from the interface by the exchange length (∼50–100 nm). Given the compositional and valence changes due to the precipitates (both the spinel phase and low-spin Co) and their relatively significant population, we anticipate enhanced magnetic frustration in the system.
